newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Malan says exchange rate policy continues.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Malan says exchange rate policy continues.

text.p: Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan said Tuesday he saw no reason to change foreign exchange rate policy and the twin band system of exchange rates.
Malan told Brazilian reporters in a briefing he was not concerned about a $5.539 billion trade deficit posted in 1996.
"The exchange rate policy in its general form has been established. We will continue to perfect the current system based on bands," he said.
Malan added, "There is no expectation of a change in foreign exchange rate policy."
Malan said 1996's trade deficit was due partly to low global commodities prices, which depressed Brazilian exports, and high gasoline prices, which boosted the value of imports.
"There is no need for Brazil to generate mega surpluses as it did in the past," he said.
Malan reiterated forecasts of 4.5-5.0 percent gross domestic product growth in 1997 and said inflation would continue to decline.
He acknowledged that January was likely to see a burst of inflation, but said the rate would come down again in February.

"We are not worried (about a peak in inflation in January)," he said. The markets expect January inflation to be as high as 2.0 percent because of fuel price increases, annual rises in school fees and other one-off items.
Malan said the greatest challenge for the government in 1997 would be to close the fiscal deficit. The operational public sector deficit is seen ending 1996 above 4.0 percent of GDP.

He also said he was sure Congress would soon get on with the job of passing key reforms of the pension system, the civil service and tax laws, which have been bogged down while all attention is focused on a bill allowing presidential re-election.
"Economic policy is independent of re-election," he said.
